open_points.subject: OwnerFormField destination mapping
open_points.text: its name, whether it belongs to the owner's request itself or to the values the owner gives
open_points.question: How does the owner interface determine the exact request or values destination populated by each field, including nested objects or tuple positions?
options: The field name is the destination key and both request and values are flat maps.
The table supplies a destination path in addition to the field name.
The owner interface owns a separate mapping from field names to destinations.
Nested or positional destinations are forbidden for owner-form fields.
consequences: A name-as-key rule is simple but cannot represent distinct nested or positional destinations without an additional naming convention.
A supplied path restores a self-contained provider-to-consumer contract but expands the facts the row must carry.
A separate interface mapping duplicates release knowledge and can drift from the provider's table.
Forbidding nested or positional destinations constrains the owner request and values models.
open_points.default_guess: Require the data provider's result to identify an unambiguous destination path for every row.

witness.initial: The owner request or its values contains two possible destinations that cannot be distinguished solely by the row's side and display/form name.
events: The data provider supplies the owner form table to the owner interface.
The owner enters text for the field and submits the form.
The owner interface constructs the request and values payload.
outcomes: One implementation treats the field name as a flat key.
Another implementation maps the same field to a nested or positional destination known only to the interface.
witness.observer: The receiving owner operation sees different payloads.

open_points.subject: OwnerFormField name uniqueness and namespace
open_points.question: Must field names be unique across the entire table, unique only within request versus values, or may duplicate names occur with another disambiguator?
options: Names are unique within each of request and values.
Duplicate names are allowed and another identifier or path disambiguates them.
consequences: Global uniqueness permits direct form lookup by name.
Side-scoped uniqueness requires the interface to preserve the request-versus-values namespace during rendering and submission.
Allowing duplicates requires an additional stable disambiguator and collision behavior.

witness.initial: One request field and one values field have the same name; the text states no uniqueness rule.
events: The data provider includes both rows in the table.
The owner interface renders both fields in one form.
The owner submits values for both names.
outcomes: One implementation rejects the table or release because names must be globally unique.
Another accepts it and scopes lookup by whether the row belongs to request or values.
witness.observer: The owner sees either a rejected release or a usable form, and the receiving operation may see different submitted values.

open_points.subject: Closed-list field vocabulary
open_points.text: as one of a closed list
open_points.question: For each closed-list field, what identifies the applicable list, where are its allowed members defined, and must the data provider expose those members to the owner interface?
options: Each row carries its allowed members.
Each row identifies a separately published enumeration or catalog.
The field name selects a list privately known to the owner interface.
All closed-list fields share one list.
consequences: Embedding members makes the table self-contained but repeats catalog data.
Referencing a published catalog requires a stable catalog identity and an additional provider obligation.
A private interface mapping duplicates release knowledge and can drift from the provider.
One shared list is only viable if every such field has the same domain.
open_points.default_guess: Have each row identify a provider-owned closed enumeration whose allowed values the owner interface can obtain.

witness.initial: The table contains a field whose text-read kind is closed-list, but no list identity or members are stated.
events: The data provider returns the row.
The owner interface renders a picker and validates the submitted selection.
outcomes: One implementation offers one set of choices inferred from the field name.
Another implementation offers a different set or cannot render the picker without a separate catalog.
witness.observer: The owner sees different choices, and the receiving operation accepts different values.

open_points.subject: Owner form table provider-to-consumer contract
open_points.text: The release: the owner form table the data provider holds.
open_points.question: What public obligation makes the provider-held table available to the owner interface, and which module owns that exported operation or constant?
options: The data provider publicly exports the table as a release constant imported by the owner interface.
The data provider owns a public accessor returning the table.
A composition root injects the table into the owner interface without a direct provider import.
The owner interface owns a copied table synchronized by release generation.
consequences: A public constant creates a direct provider-to-consumer import edge.
An accessor adds a callable boundary and its failure/effect obligations must be stated.
Injection moves delivery ownership to composition while preserving provider ownership of the data.
A copied table creates two authorities unless generation and equality obligations are defined.
open_points.default_guess: Make the data provider the sole public owner of a release constant and declare the owner interface's direct dependency on it.

witness.initial: A release contains the provider-held owner form table and the owner interface must render the corresponding fields.
events: The application initializes the owner interface.
The interface attempts to obtain the table for rendering.
outcomes: One implementation directly imports a provider export.
Another expects injection or calls an accessor, producing a different module boundary and dependency graph.
witness.observer: The generator or application composition fails unless it silently chooses the same delivery mechanism as the generated modules.

open_points.subject: OwnerFormField textual decoding
open_points.text: how its text is read: as text, as a whole number, as yes or no, or as one of a closed list.
open_points.question: Which exact textual spellings, normalization rules, and invalid-input behavior implement these already accepted read categories?
options: Define one canonical spelling for each category and reject every other spelling.
Accept specified aliases and normalize them to canonical values.
Use the form framework's native submitted representation rather than textual spellings.
consequences: Canonical spellings are deterministic but less permissive.
Aliases improve input tolerance but require explicit collision and normalization rules.
Framework-native values reduce parsing but couple the contract representation to the selected UI framework.
open_points.requirement: how its text is read: as text, as a whole number, as yes or no, or as one of a closed list.
open_points.default_guess: Specify canonical UTF-8 text forms, trim no content unless explicitly allowed, use base-10 nonnegative whole numbers, use lowercase yes/no, and reject any value outside the identified closed list.

witness.initial: A yes-or-no field is submitted with text whose representation is not fixed by the semantic category.
events: The owner interface reads the submitted field.
Its decoder applies its chosen lexical rules.
outcomes: Another accepts framework booleans or aliases such as "true" and "false".
witness.observer: The owner sees the same submission accepted by one implementation and refused by another.
